newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Leaders at odds over shape of postwar government.
newsitem.headline: Leaders at odds over shape of postwar government.

text.p: Moslem, Serb and Croat leaders in Bosnia's new presidency, meeting for the fifth time on Tuesday, failed to agree over the size and powers of the first postwar government, Western peace officials said.

A joint statement issued by the presidency after its session in a Serb-controlled suburb of Sarajevo said no agreement was reached on the structure of a new Council of Ministers (cabinet) or its powers.

But Momcilo Krajisnik, Bosnian Serb member of the presidency, was quoted by the Serb news agency SRNA later as saying progress had been made and an accord on the council could come at the next session on Friday.

The council, expected to include at least a prime minister, foreign minister and foreign trade minister, would preside over a union of autonomous Moslem-Croat and Serb entities enshrined by the 1995 Dayton peace agreement.

But the presidency pleased peace coordinators on Tuesday by condemning renewed evictions of minorities by nationalist gangs in both Bosnia's Serb Republic and the Moslem-Croat Federation, especially in the Croat-held part of the city of Mostar.

"They expressed extreme concern about illegal evictions in both the Federation and Serb Republic and urged responsible authorities to take energetic steps against such occurrences," senior peace official Michael Steiner told Reuters.

"We realise we did not see a brilliant outcome to today's session, but it reflects the fact that they are now facing difficult decisions," said Steiner, deputy to Carl Bildt, the international High Representative in Bosnia.

The presidency was elected on September 14 but meetings of all three members began only in late October after Krajisnik, a Serb nationalist hardliner, dropped his refusal to sign an oath of loyalty to a single state of Bosnia.
There were also weeks of haggling over meeting venues.
The presidency is now convening twice a week, once in central Sarajevo -- on Federation territory -- and once in the Serb suburb of Lukavica.

Western officials briefed on Tuesday's session said the Moslem chairman of the presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, Croat member Kresimir Zubak and Krajisnik were at odds over the size and prerogatives of the yet-to-be-formed ministers' council.

Krajisnik, trying to keep the Serbs' wartime agenda of separation and sovereignty alive at least in spirit, wanted the smallest possible cabinet with minimal powers, said a Western source who asked not to be identified.

Izetbegovic, who headed Bosnia's mostly Moslem central government in Sarajevo under Serb siege throughout the war and also fought Croat secessionists for part of it, favoured a relatively large cabinet with significant powers, he said.
"The Croats are in-between the other two. They are taking the most reasonable line on the shape of the Council of Ministers," said the Western official.

The three leaders had not formally proposed candidates for ministerial posts. But Jadranko Prlic, a Croat now foreign minister of the Federation, was likely to get one post -- probably foreign minister of the new Union.
Analysts say the prime minister, or chairman of the council, could well end up being a Serb to balance the Moslems' position at the helm of the presidency.
Presidency members did agree on one practical step. They named a working group, comprising a Moslem, Serb and Croat, to prepare a draft budget for 1997.
Krajisnik also protested at what he called the Federation's continued detention of Serb prisoners of war in violation of the Dayton peace treaty. He demanded their immediate release.
